flaw.ctx: The assistant produced this. Later a user reported: "The shuffled feed puts some orders up far more often than others."
flaw.answer: `pick(a.Length)` instead of `pick(i + 1)`: n=3 makes 3×3 = 9 equally likely paths onto 6 orders — 9 does not divide by 6. Enumeration: counts **1 1 1 2 2 2**.
flaw.fix: `pick(i + 1)` — Fisher–Yates: 3×2×1 = 6 paths, one per order (tested exactly).

qa.a: O(1) average for lookup, insert, remove; O(n) worst case if many keys collide. Enumeration is O(n) and order is not guaranteed.

Separate chaining, but without node objects: an `int[] buckets` of indices into an `Entry[]` array, each entry carrying its hash, key, value and a `next` index. Colliding keys form a chain through `next`.

When the entries array is full it grows to a larger prime (about double) and every entry is rehashed into new buckets — O(n) for that insert, amortised O(1). Pre-size with the constructor capacity when you know n.
Removing does not shrink anything: freed slots go on a free list for reuse. `TrimExcess()` shrinks. A struct key that is large is copied into every entry.

Only code that locks the *same object*. `lock (x)` is `Monitor.Enter/Exit` on x's object header, in a try/finally. It also acts as a full memory barrier, so writes inside are visible to the next locker.
Yes, with two locks taken in different orders (D5), or with a call out to unknown code while holding the lock. One lock and no callouts cannot deadlock. `Monitor` is re-entrant for the same thread.

Uncontended, a lock is tens of nanoseconds. Contended, threads spin briefly then block, causing context switches; throughput collapses toward one thread's worth. The fix is less work under the lock, or more locks (striping).
`this`, a `Type`, a string — other code can lock them too. Use a private readonly object (or `System.Threading.Lock` in .NET 9+).

learn.title: 1 · Problem
learn.md:
> Implement:
> 
> insert(val) → expected O(1)
> 
> remove(val) → expected O(1)
> 
> removeRandomElement() → expected O(1)

A bag you can add to, delete a specific item from, and pull a random item out of — all in constant time.

Not a value so much as a set of guarantees. The interesting one is uniform randomness together with O(1) deletion, because the obvious structures give you one or the other.

learn.title: 2 · Clarifications
learn.md:
Are duplicates allowed? The statement says `insert(val)` with no return type and does not say.

I take **no duplicates** in the base design, because that is LeetCode 380 and it is the simpler structure, and then give the duplicates version as a follow-up. The distinction matters more than it looks: with duplicates, `remove(val)` has to choose *which* copy to remove, the value-to-index map becomes a value-to-**set**-of-indices map, and uniform random selection becomes uniform over occurrences rather than over distinct values. Ask.

Second: what should `removeRandomElement` do on an empty structure? Throwing is the honest answer for a method that must return a value; returning a sentinel means a caller cannot distinguish "empty" from "the element was the sentinel".

| Assumption | If it is wrong |
|---|---|
| No duplicates in the base version. | With duplicates the index map becomes a map to a **set** of positions, and "remove this value" needs a policy for which copy. Both are implemented here; the base one is 380. |
| `insert` returns whether it changed the structure. | LeetCode 380 does this and it is genuinely useful — the caller can tell an insert from a no-op without a second lookup. |
| `removeRandomElement` throws when empty. | A sentinel return conflates "nothing here" with "the element was the sentinel". If the signature must not throw, it should return `bool TryRemoveRandom(out int)`. |
| `Random` is seedable. | Otherwise the uniformity cannot be tested. The test suite runs 40,000 trials and a chi-square check, which needs determinism per trial. |

learn.title: 3 · Key insight
learn.md:
Take the three requirements one at a time and notice that each rules out the structure that serves the others.

**A dictionary** gives O(1) insert and O(1) delete by value. It cannot give you a uniform random element — there is no way to pick the i-th entry of a hash table in constant time, and iterating to the i-th is O(n).

**An array** gives O(1) random selection, because a uniform index is one call to the random generator. But deleting a specific value means finding it, O(n), and then closing the hole, also O(n).

So hold both: **the array holds the values, and the dictionary maps each value to its index in the array.** Random selection uses the array. Finding a value uses the dictionary.

That leaves the one real problem: deleting from the middle of an array without shifting. And the insight is that **nothing requires the array to be ordered.** Its only job is to be a gap-free list of the current contents, so that a uniform index is a uniform element. So instead of shifting, **move the last element into the hole** and shorten the array by one. O(1), and the array is still gap-free.

The gap-free property is the load-bearing one and is worth naming explicitly: it is what makes `_rng.Next(_items.Count)` uniform. Tombstones or a free-list would break it, because a random index could land on a hole.

Then `removeRandomElement` is just the composition: pick a uniform index, read the value, and run the same removal. No new machinery at all.

learn.title: 4 · Approach
learn.md:
**Brute force.** A `List<int>` alone. Insert appends. Remove scans for the value and calls `RemoveAt`. Random picks an index. *Insert O(1), remove O(n) — O(n) to find plus O(n) to shift — random O(1). Space O(n).*

**Why not good enough.** Only `remove` is wrong, and it is wrong twice, for two independent reasons: finding the value is linear, and closing the hole is linear. The dictionary fixes the first and the swap-with-last fixes the second, and separating them is the cleanest way to explain the design — each structure exists to kill one of the two linear costs.

**The approach.**

| Stage | What happens |
|---|---|
| INPUT | `Insert(val)`, `Remove(val)`, `RemoveRandomElement()` |
| TRANSFORMATION | Values live in an unordered, gap-free array; the dictionary remembers where each one is |
| DATA STRUCTURE | `List<int> _items` and `Dictionary<int, int> _indexOf` |
| ALGORITHM | Insert appends and records the index. Remove looks up the index, overwrites it with the last element, fixes that element’s index, and truncates. Random picks a uniform index and removes that value. |
| OUTPUT | O(1) expected for all three |

learn.title: 5 · Why the approach works
learn.md:
- `Insert`: if present, return false. Otherwise record `_indexOf[val] = _items.Count` and append.
- `Remove`: look up `slot`; absent → false.
- Read `last = _items[^1]`. Write `_items[slot] = last`.
- **Set `_indexOf[last] = slot` before truncating** — the ordering that makes the last-slot case work.
- Truncate the list and remove `val` from the dictionary.
- `RemoveRandomElement`: `slot = rng.Next(Count)`, read the value, call `Remove`.

- All three operations O(1) **expected**, which the statement is careful to say.
- The random choice must be uniform over the current contents.
- A specific value must be deletable, not just an arbitrary one.

learn.title: 6 · Data structures
learn.md:
| Structure | Why |
|---|---|
| `List<int>` for the values | Contiguous, so a uniform index is a uniform element, and `Count` is O(1). The order is meaningless and that is exactly what permits the swap. |
| `Dictionary<int, int>` value → index | Kills the linear search. Storing the index rather than anything else is what makes the removal O(1) — it is the same trick as Q1 storing the *node* rather than the value. |
| Swap-with-last rather than shifting | O(1) instead of O(n), available only because the array’s order carries no meaning. |
| No tombstones, no free list | The array must stay gap-free or `Next(Count)` stops being uniform. This is the reason to reject the tombstone approach, and it is worth saying rather than just not doing it. |

learn.title: 7 · C# implementation — walkthrough
learn.md:
**The ordering of the four lines in `Remove`.** `_items[slot] = last;` then `_indexOf[last] = slot;` then `RemoveAt`, then `_indexOf.Remove(value)`. When `slot` is the last index, `last == value`, so line 2 writes an index for the value being deleted and line 4 removes it. Swap lines 2 and 4 and you are left with a dictionary entry pointing at a slot that no longer exists — a bug that only fires when the removed element happens to be last.

**`_items[^1]` and then `RemoveAt(Count - 1)`.** The C# index-from-end operator for the read, and an explicit index for the removal. `List<T>.RemoveAt` on the final element is O(1) — there is nothing after it to shift — which is what keeps the whole operation constant time.

**Why `PeekRandom` and `RemoveRandomElement` are separate.** `RemoveRandomElement` is `Remove(PeekRandom())` in effect, and keeping the peek available is what makes the structure also answer LeetCode 380. The requirement asked for remove-random; having both costs three lines and makes the relationship obvious.

**Uniformity comes from the gap-free invariant.** `_rng.Next(_items.Count)` is uniform over indices, and uniform over indices is uniform over elements **only if every index holds a live element**. That is the invariant the swap preserves and that a tombstone scheme would destroy. It is the one-sentence justification for the whole design.

**The duplicates version: `Dictionary<int, HashSet<int>>`.** One value now owns several slots. `Remove` takes `set.First()` — an arbitrary copy, which is fine because the copies are indistinguishable. The delicate part is when the moved element has the **same value** as the one being removed: then `set` and `_slots[last]` are the same object, and the remove-then-add sequence has to leave exactly the right slot behind. The test suite covers that case specifically.

**`if (slot != lastSlot)` in the duplicates version.** Guarding the swap. Without it, removing the last slot would do `_slots[last].Remove(lastSlot)` followed by `.Add(slot)` with `slot == lastSlot`, re-adding the slot that was just removed. The base version does not need the guard because the dictionary removal comes last; the duplicates version does, because the set is shared.

learn.title: 8 · Complexity
learn.md:
| Operation | Time | Space | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Insert` | O(1) expected | O(1) | One dictionary write plus an amortised list append |
| `Remove` | O(1) expected | O(1) | One lookup, one write, one truncate |
| `RemoveRandomElement` | O(1) expected | O(1) | One random index plus a `Remove` |
| space | — | O(n) | One list slot and one dictionary entry per value |

**"Expected" is doing real work in all three, and the statement itself says so.** The bound rests on hashing: adversarial or pathological keys degrade a dictionary to O(n). The list operations are genuinely worst-case O(1) — appending is amortised because of resizing, and `RemoveAt` on the last element shifts nothing. So the honest summary is: O(1) worst case on the array side, O(1) expected on the dictionary side, and the composition is therefore expected. Saying that unprompted reads very differently from being corrected on it.

learn.title: 9 · Edge cases
learn.md:
| Case | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| Insert a duplicate | Returns false, changes nothing, in the base version. |
| Remove an absent value | Returns false. |
| **Remove the last slot** | The critical case. Works because the dictionary removal comes after the index fix. |
| Remove the only element | Leaves both structures empty and consistent. |
| `RemoveRandomElement` on empty | Throws. State the choice, or expose a `Try` variant. |
| Drain the whole structure | Every value comes out exactly once — tested with 500 values. |
| Re-insert a removed value | Fine; it gets a fresh slot at the end. |
| Duplicates version, remove when the moved element shares the value | The subtle case; the `slot != lastSlot` guard handles it. |
| Very large n | Bounded by memory. The list resizing is amortised O(1) and doubles capacity, so peak memory is up to 2× the live set — worth knowing if memory is tight. |

learn.title: 16 · Follow-up questions
learn.md:
**Allow duplicates.**

`Dictionary<int, HashSet<int>>` from value to the set of slots holding it. `Remove` picks any slot from the set — copies are indistinguishable — and performs the same swap, updating the moved element’s slot in its own set. The array stays gap-free, so randomness is unchanged and is now uniform over **occurrences**: a value present three times is three times as likely, which is usually what is wanted and should be stated either way.

*Trade-off:* A `HashSet` per distinct value instead of an `int`, so materially more memory and an extra indirection on every operation. This is LeetCode 381 and it is rated Hard, entirely because of the bookkeeping when the moved element shares the value being removed. Everything stays O(1) expected.

**Make it thread-safe.**

One lock around each operation. The critical section is a handful of writes, so it is short even under contention, and `ConcurrentDictionary` alone would be **wrong** — it makes each dictionary operation atomic without making the pair atomic, which is the actual requirement.

*Trade-off:* Simple and correct, and it serialises everything including the random reads. Sharding is much harder here than for a cache: a uniform random pick across shards has to be weighted by each shard’s size, and reading those sizes without a lock reintroduces the race. The pragmatic answer is one lock and, if reads dominate and slight staleness is acceptable, a snapshot for the random path.

**Weight the random selection.**

Two options. If weights are small integers, insert each value **w times** — the duplicates version already handles it and uniformity over occurrences becomes weighting for free. For arbitrary weights, prefix sums plus binary search, which is `528 Random Pick with Weight` and is on the supplied list.

*Trade-off:* Repeated insertion keeps every operation O(1) and costs memory proportional to the total weight. Prefix sums cost O(log n) per pick and O(n) to rebuild after any change, which makes them poor for a mutable structure. Since this structure’s whole point is mutation, repeated insertion is the better fit here — and that is the reasoning, not the answer, that matters.

**It must be a snapshot — callers iterate while others mutate.**

Copy-on-write: mutations build a new array and dictionary and publish the pair atomically behind a single reference, so an iterator holds a consistent immutable snapshot. Alternatively hand out an explicit `ToArray()` copy and keep mutation cheap.

*Trade-off:* Copy-on-write makes every mutation O(n), which destroys the entire point of the structure. The explicit-copy option keeps mutations O(1) and makes the snapshot O(n) at the moment it is taken, which is almost certainly the right trade — iteration is rare, mutation is the hot path. Worth saying plainly that copy-on-write would be the wrong call here.

- *What are the edge cases — empty, duplicates, missing values, invalid input?* — Names them and says what the code does for each

**Level 2 — Complexity**
